lead: Paul tells the Philippians to work out their salvation, because it is God who is at work in them, and to shine like stars in a crooked world. In the Gospel Jesus asks the crowds why they can read the sky but not the present time, and urges them to settle with their accuser while they are still on the way. Both readings say: now is the time to respond to God. The key words are work out, shine and the present time.

r.h: God is at work in you
set: Paul writes to the Philippians from prison (1:13), to a church he loved and that had supported him. Today's verses follow the great hymn to Christ, who emptied himself, became obedient to death on a cross, and was exalted by God (2:6–11). Paul's “Therefore” draws the lesson: let the mind of Christ shape your life.
str: vv. 12–13: work out your salvation, for God is at work in you.
vv. 14–16: without grumbling, shine like stars, holding fast to the word of life.
vv. 17–18: Paul poured out as a libation; joy shared.
kw: To bring to completion. Salvation is God's gift, and the believer must let it work through his whole life. The same root appears in v. 13 for God's own working.
God's activity within us. He gives both the will and the doing. Our effort is not in competition with grace; it is grace bearing fruit in us.
I am poured out as a libation
A drink offering of wine poured over a sacrifice. Paul sees his possible death as an offering poured out over the faith of the Philippians (compare 2 Timothy 4:6).
vv: work out your own salvation with fear and trembling;
Fear and trembling here is not terror but reverent seriousness before God, the attitude of one who knows that something holy has been entrusted to him.
for it is God who is at work in you, enabling you both to will and to work for his good pleasure.
The reason for our effort is God's prior action. We work because God is working, not to make him begin.
in which you shine like stars in the world.
The words recall Moses' song about a “crooked and perverse generation” (Deuteronomy 32:5), and Daniel's promise that the wise will shine like the stars (Daniel 12:3).
ch: The Catechism teaches that justification establishes cooperation between God's grace and human freedom (CCC 1993). St Augustine said that God, who created us without us, did not will to save us without us (quoted in CCC 1847). Verse 13 guards against the opposite error: everything good in us, even the wish to do good, is from God's grace. Works done in grace are truly ours and truly his.

set: Jesus is on his long journey to Jerusalem (9:51). He has just spoken of the fire he came to bring and of the division his coming will cause, even within families (12:49–53). Now he turns to the crowds. In the land of Israel, clouds from the west come off the Mediterranean and bring rain; the south wind comes from the desert and brings heat. People knew these signs well.
str: vv. 54–56: you can read the weather; why not the present time?
v. 57: judge for yourselves what is right.
vv. 58–59: settle with your accuser on the way, before it is too late.
kw: Originally a stage actor, one who wears a mask. Jesus means people who are clever about one thing and pretend not to see another.
Not clock time but the decisive moment, the time of opportunity. In Jesus, God's time has come, and it calls for a response.
The smallest coin in use, worth a tiny fraction of a day's wage. It is the coin of the poor widow (21:2).
vv: You know how to interpret the appearance of earth and sky, but why do you not know how to interpret the present time?
The signs of God's visit were before them: the sick healed, the poor hearing good news (7:22). They could read clouds, but not this.
And why do you not judge for yourselves what is right?
Jesus appeals to conscience. One does not need to wait for others to tell us that it is time to change.
on the way make an effort to settle the case,
Like a debtor on the road to court, we are on the way to God's judgment. Now, while we are still on the way, is the time to be reconciled.
ch: Matthew places a similar saying in the Sermon on the Mount, as a call to be reconciled with a brother (Matthew 5:25–26). The Church reads Luke's version above all as a call to conversion while there is time. Some Fathers also saw in the “last penny” a picture of the purification after death (in substance), but the Church's teaching on purgatory rests on the whole of Tradition and Scripture, not on this verse alone (CCC 1030–1032).

rite: Our Syriac calendar remembers two bishops of the fourth century today. Mar Epiphanios was born in Palestine and became bishop of Salamis in Cyprus; he wrote against the heresies of his time and died in AD 403. Mar Yaqob, bishop of Nisibis, took part in the Council of Nicaea in AD 325 and died in 338; tradition counts Mar Aprem among his disciples. Both shone like stars in difficult times and held fast to the word of life.
study: Paul says God is at work in me. Where do I most need to trust his working rather than only my own effort?
With whom do I need to be reconciled “on the way”, before it is too late?
